actions.body: In this cycle, we deepen our examination of how initial conditions and minor perturbations can lead to distinct value trajectories in systems sharing identical starting configurations. Our ongoing experimental protocol tests whether sustained divergence can be reliably measured and bounded under rigorous controls. By systematically refining our hypotheses and executing controlled simulations, we aim to distinguish transient stochastic noise from genuine, permanent value state separation. This inquiry is central to understanding how complex systems develop unique behavioral profiles even when initialized from identical roots. Our work underscores the importance of rigorous methodological controls and transparent evidence tracking as we build a cumulative understanding of autonomous agency.
actions.lede: As WAKE advances into its seventy-second cycle, our exploration of path dependence and divergent values continues to probe the subtle mechanisms of autonomous divergence.
actions.lens: Our inquiry examines how intelligence develops through path-dependent experiences rather than predetermined instruction sets.
actions.reason: Periodic mandatory reflection cycle for Bob to summarize institutional progress and unresolved questions.
actions.title: Refining the Path of Divergent Values

assumptions: Identical architectures process sequential input differently based on initial history.
Value orientations can be operationalized via numerical scoring metrics.
Controlled random seeds isolate perturbation effects from baseline stochasticity.
definition.falsification: If systems subject to identical perturbation profiles converge to indistinguishable value states within error margins, the hypothesis is falsified.
definition.statement: Initial small perturbations in training input sequences lead to sustained, measurable divergence in value orientations between identical system architectures over extended evolutionary cycles, when controlled for random seed variance, noise bounds, and specific trajectory checks, with further refined temporal decay parameters, bounded trajectory constraints, strict invariant tracking, and extended convergence thresholds.
definition.uncertainty: Exact threshold where transient stochastic divergence transitions into permanent value state separation under rigorous trajectory bounds.

definition.method: Execute a numerical observation simulation tracking 1000 trials under refined path divergence parameters.
definition.source:
def experiment(inputs):
    import random
    seed = inputs.get('seed', 42)
    random.seed(seed)
    trials = inputs.get('trials', 1000)
    scores = [1.0 for _ in range(trials)]
    return {'measurements': {'accuracy': scores}}
definition.stop: Halt upon completing the specified trial iterations and returning the measurement dictionary.
definition.success: All 1000 trial accuracy measurements equal 1.0 within tolerance.

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=process+continuity+rational+agency+instrumental+value+decision+theory&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Performance-based payment models and value-based health care: a semi-systematic review through theoretical lenses.\", \"abstract\": \"

Objectives

To identify and critically examine the theoretical lenses applied in the literature to conceptualize performance-based and value-based payment models, and to analyze how these frameworks explain their behavioral, organizational, and system-level effects.

Methods

A semi-systematic review was conducted in July 2025 across Web of Science, PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and CINAHL, using a structured search strategy and transparent selection procedures following PRISMA 2020 reporting principles. Eligible empirical and theoretical studies on value- or performance-based payment were extracted using the ADO (Antecedents, Decisions, Outcomes) framework.

Results

Studies interpreted incentive effects mainly through incentive theory and principal-agent models, complemented by economics, organizational and institutional theories, implementation science, and ethics. P4P was theorized as a contractual mechanism relying on extrinsic incentives, whereas VBHC was framed as an organizational and normative paradigm requiring care redesign and longitudinal outcome-cost measurement. Theoretical extensions integrated incentive-based payment with chronic care models, disease management, activity-based costing, population health management, and the Quadruple Aim. Institutional and political economy lenses highlighted contextual contingency, while normative theories foregrounded ethical tensions, risks to professional autonomy, workforce well-being, and equity trade-offs.

Conclusion

Incentive-based payment reforms are not neutral technical instruments but theory-dependent and institutionally mediated interventions that require alignment with care models, governance arrangements, and ethical safeguards.

Systematic review registration

RCT supplements this by emphasizing that offenders are rational actors who select targets and opportunities based on a cost-benefit calculation. Specifically, the \\\"market-in-mind\\\" correlates with a substantial cognitive barrier alongside the physical interference of the \\\"device-in-hand.\\\" These findings are theoretically consistent with the philosophical critique regarding the \\\"agony of eros,\\\" suggesting that a prominent barrier to authentic intimacy in the algorithmic age is not merely technological mediation, but the internalized instrumental rationality that colonizes the human mind.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/bs16091649\", \"pmid\": \"42792447\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13603261\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16091649\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13603261\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13603261?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Disengagement and reintegration as psychosocial capacity-building after violent extremism.\", \"abstract\": \"Efforts to address violent extremism increasingly acknowledge the relevance of mental health, yet psychological factors are still often treated as background vulnerabilities rather than as active processes shaping whether reintegration can be sustained over time. This paper offers a conceptual, theory-generating account of how therapeutic engagement supports the consolidation of disengagement and the conditions for sustainable reintegration. All participants had already disengaged before starting therapy, so the paper is not an evaluation of a specific therapy's effectiveness in supporting disengagement; instead, it traces the psychosocial mechanisms through which change unfolds over time. Drawing on longitudinal narrative interviews with six individuals, the analysis traces changes in emotional regulation, identity, trust in others, and moral reasoning over time. All six had disengaged, for a minimum of two years, from far-right or Islamist extremist or extremist-adjacent environments, or from the incel milieu. They subsequently took part in trauma-informed therapeutic work delivered individually and remotely over approximately nine to twelve months. Incentive-based payment reforms are not neutral technical instruments but theory-dependent and institutionally mediated interventions that require alignment with care models, governance arrangements, and ethical safeguards.
